title: Wealth That Does No Good
note: This is the nature of wealth that is no use to the one who earned it or to anyone else. The owner’s fault is laid on the wealth. The last couplet of the previous chapter pointed here.

couplets.plain: He stores up great heaps of wealth and doesn’t eat from it. He is a dead man, and there is nothing he can do with it.
couplets.pm: A man who piles up wealth enough to fill his house and, from greed, doesn’t enjoy it is dead though he lives, because he has no claim on it. “Eating” means enjoying it with all five senses. It can also mean that if he dies without enjoying it he has no claim, so enjoy wealth when you get it.

links.quote: stores up great heaps of wealth and doesn’t eat from it
there is nothing he can do with it

couplets.plain: “Wealth brings everything,” you think, and you clutch it and give nothing. That delusion brings a wretched birth.
couplets.pm: You know that wealth alone brings everything, and you earn it. Then you grip it and give nothing, and from that confusion comes a ghost’s birth that is never filled. You watched others go hungry with wealth to hand, so you will be born to suffer hunger with food all around you.

links.quote: That delusion brings a wretched birth
links.reason: Promises a wretched birth to anyone who takes wealth for everything and gives nothing.

couplets.plain: Men who crave piling up wealth and don’t want fame are only a load on the earth.
couplets.pm: People who want only to earn more than others, and don’t want the fame that is its fruit, are born to be a burden on the land. Fame is righteousness that serves in both worlds. They don’t seek it by giving, and in their ignorance choose the pain of earning and guarding.

links.quote: crave piling up wealth and don’t want fame
only a load on the earth

couplets.plain: What does he think he will leave behind, this man whom no one wants?
couplets.pm: A man no one wants, because he has never given anything: what does he imagine will remain here after he dies? The fame that remains stays only with those who give, so he has nothing to do with it.

links.quote: What does he think he will leave behind

couplets.plain: People who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, even with ten million heaped on ten million.
couplets.pm: Those who neither give to others nor enjoy it themselves have nothing, even with many millions stacked up. Giving is named first because righteousness stands above pleasure. They lose both fruits, so they are like people who have nothing.

links.quote: have nothing, even with ten million heaped on ten million
links.reason: Whoever neither gives nor enjoys has nothing, however high the heap.

links.quote: neither give nor enjoy have nothing

couplets.plain: A man who won’t enjoy it himself and has no habit of giving to the deserving is a sickness to great wealth.
couplets.pm: A man who doesn’t enjoy his wealth, and by nature gives the worthy nothing they ask for, is a sickness to great wealth, which could have done both. The worthy are those fit to receive gifts. Some say instead that his great wealth brings him only the pain of earning and guarding it.

links.quote: won’t enjoy it himself and has no habit of giving to the deserving
links.reason: Such an owner harms the wealth he holds, neither tasting it nor sharing it.
Makes the man himself an illness that great wealth has caught.

couplets.plain: The wealth of a man who gives nothing to those who have nothing is like a woman of great beauty growing old alone.
couplets.pm: The wealth of a man who gives the destitute nothing they need passes away for nothing. A woman of rare beauty and goodness, whom no one gave in marriage, grows old alone without a husband. As her own life is wasted, and not only her family’s hopes and a husband’s, so the wealth’s use is lost as well as the owner’s and the receiver’s.
couplets.sensitive: likens a woman who ages unmarried to wasted wealth

links.quote: gives nothing to those who have nothing
links.reason: Wealth that never reaches the needy withers unused, as beauty does when it grows old alone.

couplets.plain: The wealth of a man no one wants is like a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village.
couplets.pm: A man lives close to the poor but gives them nothing, so they want nothing from him. His gaining wealth is like a poison tree ripening in the middle of the village. Being near and having plenty are no use.

links.quote: a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village

couplets.plain: You give up loving-kindness, punish yourself and ignore righteousness to gather bright wealth, and others take it.
couplets.pm: To avoid giving, he drops loving-kindness for kin and friends, denies himself what he needs, and gives no thought to righteousness such as giving to the poor. Others carry off the bright wealth he gathered and get the use of it. Without righteousness or pleasure, gathering is only pain, and it doesn’t even serve his own line.

links.quote: to gather bright wealth, and others take it
links.reason: Punishing yourself and ignoring loving-kindness and righteousness only gathers wealth for others to take.

couplets.plain: A short spell of hardship for the wealthy of good name is like a rain cloud running dry.
couplets.pm: The poverty of those with wealth and fame lasts only a little while, like the cloud that sustains the world growing poor. Those who helped everyone soon recover and help again, so wealth that does no good never helps at all. He rejects the reading that this is about the rich tiring of beggars, which doesn’t fit the chapter.

links.quote: A short spell of hardship for the wealthy of good name
links.reason: Sets the rich of good name beside the rain cloud, the great giver, whose shortage doesn’t last.

links.quote: like a rain cloud running dry
links.reason: A person of good name run dry is only a rain cloud that will fill again.
